findings.source_passage: Thereupon little Giry--the girl with eyes black as sloes, hair black as ink, a swarthy complexion and a poor little skin stretched over poor little bones--little Giry added: 'If that's the ghost, he's very ugly!'
findings.source_locator: after Jammes drops into a chair, before 'And they all began to talk together'
findings.why_it_matters: The physical portrait of little Giry mirrors and contrasts the portrait of Jammes; both descriptions are stylistically distinctive parallel constructions that establish the two girls as recurring characters. Giry's line 'If that's the ghost, he's very ugly!' is also the chapter's first note of dark comedy. Both are absent from the draft.
findings.suggested_fix: Restore the full character description of little Giry and her line verbatim before the girls begin talking together.

findings.source_passage: one of them, who had more or less kept her head. 'You see the ghost everywhere!'
findings.source_locator: after the girls describe the ghost appearing in the passage, before the narrator's long aside on ghost legend
findings.why_it_matters: This skeptical interjection provides the ironic counterweight that the narrator then immediately undercuts with his long satirical aside about how the legend swelled; removing it flattens the setup-and-reversal rhetorical structure.
findings.suggested_fix: Restore the dissenting girl's line as a beat before the narrator's aside on ghost legend growth.

findings.source_passage: Had any one met with a fall, or suffered a practical joke at the hands of one of the other girls, or lost a powderpuff, it was at once the fault of the ghost, of the Opera ghost.
findings.source_locator: within the narrator's aside on the ghost legend, after 'those who laughed the loudest were not the most at ease'
findings.why_it_matters: The tricolon climaxing on 'lost a powderpuff' is Leroux's comic-ironic voice at its most characteristic — escalating from injury to petty inconvenience, ending with 'of the ghost, of the Opera ghost' as a mock-solemn refrain. Its excision removes a signature voice moment.
findings.suggested_fix: Restore the sentence including 'lost a powderpuff' and the doubled 'of the ghost, of the Opera ghost' closing beat.

findings.source_passage: she flung herself upon the farthest corner of the wall, with every mark of real terror on her face, whispered: 'Listen!'
findings.source_locator: after 'An agonizing silence now reigned in the dressing-room' and before the rustling description
findings.why_it_matters: Jammes's pantomime of terror — flinging herself to the wall before whispering 'Listen!' — is a carefully staged theatrical beat that builds suspense before the silk-on-panel sound. The draft jumps straight from silence to the sound, losing Jammes's body-language moment entirely.
findings.suggested_fix: Insert Jammes's action and whispered 'Listen!' as a discrete beat between the silence and the description of the rustling.

findings.source_passage: that little dried plum of a Meg Giry, heroically holding Sorelli back by her gauze skirt. 'Whatever you do, don't open the door! Oh, Lord, don't open the door!'
findings.source_locator: after Sorelli asks 'Is there any one behind the door?'
findings.why_it_matters: 'That little dried plum of a Meg Giry' is a signature character epithet — comic, affectionate, precise — and 'heroically holding Sorelli back' is Leroux's ironic register at its best. The draft reduces this to 'Meg Giry clutched her gauze skirt,' stripping both the epithet and the ironic adverb.
findings.suggested_fix: Restore 'that little dried plum of a Meg Giry, heroically holding Sorelli back' and Meg's doubled cry 'don't open the door!' verbatim.

findings.source_locator: as the ballet-girls retreat to the inner dressing-room when Sorelli opens the door
findings.why_it_matters: This small line is Meg's comic reflex — invoking her mother as a talisman of safety — and seeds the motif of Mme. Giry's importance before her dramatic entrance. Its omission is minor but removes a planted motif.
findings.suggested_fix: Restore Meg's 'Mother! Mother!' as the girls retreat.

findings.source_passage: So this is an event which M. Moncharmin thinks natural. A man hangs at the end of a rope; they go to cut him down; the rope has disappeared. Oh, M. Moncharmin found a very simple explanation! Listen to him:
findings.source_locator: narrator's commentary immediately after the Moncharmin quotation, before the Moncharmin explanation about the ballet girls
findings.why_it_matters: This is the narrator's sarcastic framing voice — 'Oh, M. Moncharmin found a very simple explanation! Listen to him:' — before quoting the absurd explanation. The draft fuses the sections, losing the ironic drumroll introduction that is part of Leroux's comic-conspiratorial narrator persona.
findings.suggested_fix: Restore the narrator's transitional sarcastic commentary ('So this is an event which M. Moncharmin thinks natural…Oh, M. Moncharmin found a very simple explanation! Listen to him:') before the ballet-girls explanation.

summary: The draft preserves most verbatim set-pieces but erases three or more medium-severity voice moments—Giry's character portrait and comic line, Jammes's 'Listen!' staging beat, the powderpuff ironic tricolon, and the 'little dried plum' epithet—collectively flattening Leroux's comic-ironic narrator voice enough to require regeneration.
